voice: questions and support row titles sentence case; answers lowercase-plain, honest about limits; proper nouns keep their casing

questions.q: What can it detect, and what can it not?
questions.a:
it detects known wifi and bluetooth signatures from some ALPR gear, Remote ID drones, body cams, and separated trackers, plus experimental signatures for recording glasses. turn on the network cameras detector to flag nearby broadcasts from supported camera vendors. you can also star an exact device address to watch for it even when it has no known signature. starring a recognized device doesn't change its category.

it can't detect wired, passive, cellular-only, or 5 GHz-only gear. wifi scanning uses 2.4 GHz and cycles through channels, so it can miss a short broadcast. the beacon's dedicated bluetooth scanner listens continuously when it's enabled. an empty screen means no recognizable device was broadcasting in range, not that nothing is there.

questions.q: Can I turn individual detectors on or off?
questions.a: yes. open Beacon, then detectors. turning a detector category on or off changes what the beacon reports right away, and the setting stays after a restart. flock/ALPR, drones, body cams, and glasses are on by default. trackers and network cameras are off by default because they can be noisy in everyday places. scan radios lets you turn off bluetooth or wifi scanning completely.

questions.q: Why do the Status count, radar dots, and category counts differ?
questions.a:
Status shows devices heard in the last 45 seconds, excluding muted devices and offline replays. the total counts matched or watched devices separately from the ambient devices that desert mode reports. a firmware category the app doesn't recognize is shown separately as unclassified and isn't treated as ordinary nearby gear. a starred device is counted once in the total, and starring doesn't change a recognized device's category.

to keep the radar readable, it draws at most 14 dots. starred devices and recognized matches are drawn first. this limit doesn't affect the count, what gets recorded, or the Log. dots show signal strength, not direction or exact distance.

the strongest recent match card shows the device's name and how long ago it was last heard. if there's no match, the card shows an unclassified or ambient device and labels it that way. if you turn off a detector, its recent count stays visible with an OFF label until those sightings age out. tap a category with a count above zero to open the Log filtered to that category. if a category is empty and its detector is off, tapping it opens the detector setting.

questions.q: Where are everyday controls, and what do the Beacon status labels mean?
questions.a:
the Beacon tab has two views, and you switch between them at the top: BOARD, and a view for this phone (THIS PHONE, or THIS IPHONE on an iPhone). the board view has scan radios, detectors, desert mode and the offline buffer, alerts, the board LED, firmware, and managed devices. the phone view has phone notifications, Live Mode, display preferences, System readiness, improve detection, and help and support. phone notifications, which you set per category, work separately from the beacon's buzzer or silent setting.

the status labels for connecting, reconnecting, securing the link, and waiting for board status don't mean a scanning session is active. if the app can't read radio status, the radio summary shows it as unavailable instead of showing both radios as on. if the bluetooth scanner has a fault, wifi scanning can still work. detection may pause during a firmware update.

a banner appears at the top of the Beacon tab, above BOARD, when a firmware update is available, while one is in progress, and after one finishes or fails. tap it for details, including whether a second-radio update only partly finished. the rest of the time, Firmware under BOARD shows the installed version. if it says LATEST KNOWN, the app checked only the firmware catalog it already has, so a newly published update may not have been downloaded yet.

questions.q: How do I mute or ignore a device I already know about?
questions.a:
open the detection from the Log or Map and tap mute. you can mute it permanently, for 1 hour, for 24 hours, or only at this place (within 50 meters). while the mute is on, the app doesn't alert you about that device, hides it from live views, and shows its earlier detections in the Log with a muted label. muting removes its star, and starring a muted device unmutes it. use select mode (Select in the Log tools menu) to mute several devices permanently. muted devices are listed under managed devices on the Beacon tab, where you can rename or unmute them.

permanent mutes are copied to the beacon. they silence its hardware alerts and keep working when your phone isn't connected. timed and place mutes stay on the phone, because the beacon has no clock or GPS to apply them reliably. they only work while the phone is connected, and the beacon can still beep, depending on your alerts setting. a mute applies to one exact hardware address, so phones, tags, glasses, and other devices that rotate addresses can reappear under a new one. the mute list holds up to 256 devices.

questions.q: What does muting the beacon silence?
questions.a:
the alerts setting under Beacon has three modes. in buzzer mode, the board plays a sound for each new detection that qualifies for an alert, and the sound depends on the detector category. detections that arrive close together can share one sound, so not every detection beeps. vibrate and silent both turn off the board's detection sounds. vibrate makes your phone vibrate instead, with a cooldown between alerts. on Android, vibration respects Do Not Disturb. on iPhone, your phone vibrates while the app is open, even when a Focus is on. this setting controls the board's own sounds and is separate from muting a single device you already know about. phone notifications are set per category under Beacon. they are off by default and can still arrive in silent mode.

a muted board also skips its startup sound. on an always-on unit, power coming back after an outage looks the same as someone turning it on, and a muted board shouldn't make noise at 3am. two sounds still play by design when the board is muted. the shutdown sound plays, so you can hear the board turn off. on the rev-B battery model with the button, the start beep plays only when you press and hold the button to turn the board on. the only way to silence every sound the board makes is to set master volume to 0, so the volume slider is available in all three modes. the LED keeps flashing at volume 0 unless you also turn on lights out.

the board stores whether it is muted. if a change from the app doesn't reach the board, the app and the board can get out of sync. the app compares your mode with the mode the board reports in every status update. if you chose vibrate or silent and the board reports that sound is on, the app resends the setting right away, then about every 30 seconds until they match. if you chose buzzer and the board stays muted, the app stops resending and shows silent for the rest of the session. this is expected, and your saved setting doesn't change.

trackers never beep on the board in any mode, and desert mode sets the board to silent while it runs. turning desert mode off yourself restores your previous alert mode, unless you picked a mode by hand (including silent) while desert mode was running. when the board ends desert mode on its own (after a factory reset, on an older board, or because another paired phone ended it), the app doesn't change your alert mode. if this phone saved a mode when desert mode started, the app offers to restore it: a Restore Alerts control appears on the desert card under Beacon, and under alerts when that section is shown. nothing changes until you tap it. the offer stays after app restarts. it moves to the top of the Beacon tab when board controls are unavailable, and to the connect screen when the app is scanning for a beacon again, so you can tap it with the beacon off or not connected.

questions.q: What is Live Mode, and how do I put it on my lock screen?
questions.a:
Live Mode shows a count of nearby detections that you can check at a glance. it covers detections from about the last 45 seconds, the same as the Status screen, and keeps the phone connected to the beacon in the background. it is on by default after first setup, and it starts once your phone is connected to a real beacon and the permissions and system features it needs are ready. you can turn it off under Beacon. lock-screen counts are on by default, and a switch under Beacon hides them so the lock screen only says Live Mode is active. counts stay visible inside the app either way.

on android, that switch affects three places: the Live Mode card on the lock screen changes to 'Live Mode active', a detection alert no longer names its category on the lock screen, and the android 16 status-bar chip hides its running count whether the phone is locked or not. on iphone it affects the lock-screen card only. the Dynamic Island and the Watch and CarPlay views keep showing counts, and your Show Previews setting controls whether a detection alert shows its text on a locked screen.

on iphone, Live Mode appears as a Live Activity on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, with compact versions on supported Watch and CarPlay setups. on android it appears as an ongoing notification or Live Update. home-screen widgets and compatible car widgets are separate from Live Mode. add the beacons widget from your system's widget picker (on android, System readiness under Beacon can also add it for you). the widget uses a different count by design: every detection first heard today, reset at local midnight, instead of the last 45 seconds. the icon row under that number only covers categories that have an icon, so it can add up to less than the number above it. detections replayed from the offline buffer count only if the beacon has a timestamp that shows they happened today. replayed detections without a usable timestamp are left out of both the number and the icon row. your phone's operating system controls whether Live Mode and the widget can appear, so if one is missing, check System readiness under Beacon.

the first time you connect a beacon, the app shows a setup checklist. from the checklist, or right after you close it, the app may ask for the phone permission Live Mode needs. if you skip it, detection and the Log keep working, but Live Mode does not appear on the lock screen until you allow it. the System readiness row under Beacon shows what is still missing.

questions.q: Can I flag one specific device to keep an eye on?
questions.a:
yes. open any detection and tap Watch to star it. to watch a device that has no known signature, turn on desert mode, find it, star it, then turn desert mode off again. rename it in managed devices under Beacon so the Log shows your name for it. if a starred device matches a built-in signature, it keeps that category. the beacon reports it as a watched device only when no built-in signature matches. the beacon never beeps for tracker-category detections, even starred ones.

the Log and Map show a Watched category only when they contain matching detections. the Watched category includes currently starred devices in other categories and detections originally reported as watched. a starred device with no detections in the Log does not add a map pin or an empty category.

the watchlist is stored on the beacon, stays saved after a reboot, and holds up to 256 devices. it matches the exact hardware address, so it may stop matching phones, separated trackers, and other devices that rotate their address. the app warns you when that is likely.

questions.q: What is desert mode, and when would I use it?
questions.a:
normally the beacon reports devices that match a supported signature or a watched address. desert mode also reports ordinary nearby devices, such as phones, watches, earbuds, and TVs. use it to check that scanning works, explore areas with few devices, or find an unknown device to star or capture as a possible new signature. it's off by default and meant to be temporary.

a busy street can produce thousands of detections, so turn it off when you're done. it doesn't list every nearby device: radio limits, address rotation, deduplication, and rate limits still apply. desert mode sets the board to silent while it runs. turning desert mode off yourself restores your previous alert mode, unless you picked a mode by hand (including silent) while desert mode was running. when the board ends desert mode on its own (after a factory reset, on an older board, or because another paired phone ended it), the app doesn't change your alert mode. if this phone saved a mode when desert mode started, the app offers to restore it: a Restore Alerts control appears on the desert card under Beacon, and under alerts when that section is shown. nothing changes until you tap it. the offer stays after app restarts. it moves to the top of the Beacon tab when board controls are unavailable, and to the connect screen when the app is scanning for a beacon again, so you can tap it with the beacon off or not connected.

questions.q: Does desert mode cap how much it logs?
questions.a:
the app keeps a rolling window of up to 5,000 detections, in both normal and desert mode. when it is full, the oldest rows are removed and new detections keep coming in. export anything you need to keep before a long session. the limit controls how much is stored. it does not guarantee that the map stays fast with thousands of markers on every phone.

the standard offline buffer records while your phone is not connected. it skips uncategorized nearby devices in desert mode. it also cannot restore rows already removed from the app's live Log, so it is not extra storage when the Log is full.

questions.q: How do Log search, sorting, pause, and exports work?
questions.a:
you can search the Log by broadcast or custom name, vendor, or a full or partial hardware address. the control at the top of the Log shows active (heard in the last 45 seconds, not counting offline replays), new (not seen yet), or all. the Log tools menu (the sliders button) sets the sort (newest or strongest signal), a category filter, and Offline Only, which shows only detections replayed from the offline buffer. a category or Offline Only filter shows as a chip under the control. tap the chip to clear it. strongest sorts by raw RSSI, not by the confidence percentage. with the newest sort, the all and new views group rows under 'heard in the last 45 s', 'earlier today', and 'older'.

the same menu has Pause Live Feed, which freezes the Log on screen so you can look through it. the app keeps receiving and recording detections while the feed is paused. CSV and GPX exports contain the same rows as the Log you are viewing, in the same sort order, even when it is paused. CSV exports can include rows without a position, but GPX needs usable coordinates. to export every row the app currently holds, resume the live feed, clear the search, the category filter, and Offline Only, then choose all.

regular Log exports can contain the location where each detection was recorded and a drone's aircraft or operator coordinates. the location-removal switches in improve detection do not apply to them. check the file and who you are sending it to before you share it.

questions.q: Why does the Map show fewer detections, and how can I keep it responsive?
questions.a:
the control at the top of the Map sets how far back it looks: active is the last 45 seconds, recent (the default) is the last 15 minutes, and all includes older sightings and sightings with no time recorded. category filters, mutes, and missing coordinates can also hide a pin. these filters only change what the Map shows. they do not pause recording or delete anything from the Log. opening a detection in the Map from its details switches the Map to all, but muted devices stay hidden.

when the Map is crowded or zoomed out, it groups nearby pins into clusters, where one symbol stands for several detections, and can show simpler markers. zoom in for more detail. the legend first shows how many detections are on the map and how many have no location. after that, it shows how many match the current filters, how many in your stored history have a location, and whether the view is simplified.

for a busy desert-mode session, use recent or active, filter to the category you need, and turn off the known ALPR cameras layer or phone breadcrumb trails in Map options if you do not need them. trails are off by default. turning off trail display does not stop breadcrumb collection. turn off desert mode when you finish looking for unknown devices.

questions.q: Where is a tracker's breadcrumb trail, and does muting erase it?
questions.a:
open the tracker in the Log to see its breadcrumb trail on the detail map. each point marks where your phone was when the beacon heard that same tracker address, not the tracker's own GPS route. the first point needs a fresh location from your phone. after that, the app adds a point only when at least 60 seconds have passed and your phone has moved at least 25 meters. the app keeps up to 120 points per tracker in memory for the current session only, so trails are not restored after you restart the app. trails on the main Map are off by default. to show them, turn on phone breadcrumb trails in Map options. the app collects the points either way.

muting or ignoring that tracker stops the app from adding new points while the mute is active and hides its pin from the main Map. it does not erase stored Log history or the trail recorded this session in Log details. when you unmute it, the app adds points again but does not backfill the time it was muted. silent alert mode and Focus or Do Not Disturb affect alerts only and do not stop breadcrumb collection.

the Seen with you panel summarizes what the app recorded this session and does not tell you whether you are being stalked. a missing location, sparse sightings, or a rotating address can leave gaps or split one physical tag into separate detections.

questions.q: Can I leave it recording without my phone?
questions.a:
yes, with the offline buffer, which is off by default. when you turn it on, the beacon keeps logging detections while your phone is away. it stores them encrypted in its own flash memory and replays them to your phone when you reconnect with the matching key and the sync completes. storage is limited, so older records can eventually be overwritten. to show only those buffered detections, turn on Offline Only in the Log tools menu.

a transmitter that broadcasts large numbers of fake camera or drone identities cannot overwrite the buffer in minutes. the beacon limits how fast it stores recognized detections: a burst of 256, then about one every 10 seconds, with the last few slots reserved for devices it has been hearing for at least 10 seconds. if the beacon ever refuses to store detections because of that limit, the Log and the offline buffer control under Beacon show DETECTION FLOOD REFUSED to warn you that some real detections may be missing. the warning stays after a restart until the board buffer is erased.

your phone sends the beacon the encryption key. while the offline buffer is on, the beacon keeps a copy of that key in flash so it can continue recording after a reboot. the encryption does not protect the buffer if the beacon is seized. anyone who has the board can read what it stored. turning off the offline buffer stops capture and erases the board's key, but it does not erase the stored records. to delete those records, use the separate Erase control in the offline buffer section under Beacon. clearing the Log on your phone does not delete them. in standard mode, the beacon erases the buffer automatically if it is not synced to your phone within about six restarts.

if the app says BUFFER KEY NOT ACCEPTED, the history on the board is still there, but it was not sent to this phone. reconnect with the original phone and its matching key. if you are OK with losing that history, you can erase the board buffer instead, and after that the beacon buffers new detections for this phone.

the beacon has no GPS of its own, so offline detections use the last location fix your phone sent before it disconnected. the beacon stops using that fix once it is about 18 hours old. detections recorded after that still show what was detected, but with no position: no pin on the map and empty location columns in an export. the fix is kept in memory only, so if the beacon restarts while you are away, it has no location to attach until your phone reconnects. offline pins show where your phone last was, not where the beacon is. they are correct while the beacon stays in one place. if you carry it around without your phone, every offline pin shows that one location. a replayed detection either includes that fix and how old the fix was, or has no position at all.

questions.q: I can't find or pair my beacon. What should I try?
questions.a:
start with the basic checks. power the beacon with a known-good USB cable or turn it on, keep it within a few feet of your phone, and make sure Bluetooth is on. allow Nearby devices on android or Bluetooth on iphone. on older android phones, allow Location when asked, because the operating system requires it for scanning. tap Scan for Beacons, choose your beacon, then approve the pairing request on your phone if one appears.

if the scan finds nothing, wait for the beacon to finish starting up and scan again. if pairing does not finish, keep the beacon powered and nearby, cancel, and try again. if the beacon is already paired to another phone, turn the beacon off and on, then connect the new phone within two minutes. if it still fails, email support@soyboi.tech.

questions.q: My other phone won't connect to the beacon
questions.a:
once a beacon is paired to a phone, it accepts a new phone only in the first two minutes after a full power cycle. turn the beacon off and on, then connect the new phone within two minutes. the paired phone can always reconnect. a beacon that has never been paired is not affected.

this prevents someone nearby from pairing with your beacon and reading where you have been. a restart after a firmware update does not count as a power cycle.

questions.q: My beacon keeps restarting, or the startup sound plays over and over
questions.a:
this is usually caused by the cable, not the beacon. the USB-C port is recessed, so a plug can feel seated without making full contact. push the plug firmly and straight in until it stops.

if alerts are set to vibrate or silent, the beacon skips its startup sound, so a restart loop makes no sound. if lights out is off, watch the LED instead. it repeats the startup flashes on every restart, and the slow idle heartbeat only starts once the beacon stays up.

if pushing the plug in firmly does not fix it, try a slimmer plug, a known-good cable, and a wall charger instead of a power bank. if it still restarts with a known-good cable and a wall charger, email me and i'll sort it out.

questions.q: My AirTag is right next to me, why isn't the beacon flagging it?
questions.a:
first make sure trackers are turned on under Beacon. they're off by default. when an AirTag is near its owner's Apple devices, it can broadcast in an owner-connected mode, and the beacon ignores that broadcast to reduce everyday noise. the tracker signature only matches once the tag is away from its owner and sends a supported separated broadcast.

to test it, keep the tag away from all of its owner's Apple devices, give it time to switch to its separated broadcast, then bring the beacon near it. don't count on a fixed fifteen-minute wait. Tile and Samsung tags use different broadcasts and don't follow the same timing. if the beacon detects nothing, that doesn't prove no tracker is there.

questions.q: Why did it take a while before a tracker on me showed up?
questions.a:
first check that trackers are turned on under Beacon. they're off by default. once a tag sends a supported separated broadcast, the beacon reports the tag to the connected app from the first broadcast it hears. the standard offline buffer does not record a tracker until a minute after the beacon first hears it, so a tag that passes by quickly can show up in the connected app but not in the buffer.

tracker-category detections never beep on the board, even when you star them. starring a recognized tracker does not move it to the watched category. phone notifications for trackers have their own switch under Beacon and are also off by default. a notification is not an automated stalking alert.

tracker details can show when and where the same address was heard, as far as location and session limits allow. tags can rotate their addresses, so the same physical tag can show up later as a new detection.

questions.q: A tracker keeps coming back as a new device on the same trip. Is that me or someone following me?
questions.a:
most of the time it's a device that travels with you. for AirTags and Google tags, the beacon flags only the separated-from-owner broadcast, so by design it skips a phone or earbuds that are still connected to their owner. the beacon has no such check for Tile and Samsung tags and matches on their finding broadcast alone, so a Tile or Samsung tag that travels with its own owner still shows up. an Apple device that goes offline also sends the separated broadcast. that broadcast includes a byte that marks the device as a tag or a phone. the device sets that byte itself, and a tracker can set it to any value, so the beacon ignores it and treats every separated broadcast the same way.

the addresses also rotate, so one device can show up as many rows. a separated tag keeps the same address for about a day, so a star or mute on it keeps working for that time. a device that is only offline rotates much more often. on one of our own drives, a single Apple device in the car showed up as ten different addresses in just under two and a half hours, switching to a new address every fifteen minutes. a mute on the old address does not apply to the new ones.

look at the pattern across several rows. a device that travels with you has a steady, strong signal for the whole trip and shows up as a series of new addresses at a regular interval. a device you passed shows up once or twice with a weak signal and does not come back. the Seen with you panel summarizes the session. it is not a verdict, and a regular interval does not prove that a device is yours.

the tracker category is off by default under Beacon. if you don't want tracker detections during a trip, turning off the tracker category is more reliable than muting addresses that will rotate anyway.

questions.q: What does the match percentage mean, and why does a 'Strong match' still say verify?
questions.a:
the percentage measures how specific the evidence is. it is not the probability that a device is nearby, and it does not tell you how close the device is. under 50 shows as 'Weak match, verify' with an amber warning mark, 50 to 79 is 'Partial match', and 80 and up is 'Strong match'.

the 'matched on' row under MATCH QUALITY shows what matched: a broadcast name, a manufacturer ID, a service UUID, a wifi network name, a Remote ID broadcast, or only the hardware address block. the strongest matches come from devices that identify themselves. for example, a Remote ID drone broadcasts its own serial number. a starred device always matches, because you starred that exact address. the star is your own record and does not count as new evidence.

a detection can show 'Strong match' and still be flagged. the 'matched on' row tells you why. an address-block match gets an amber mark at any percentage, because the block alone cannot tell you exactly what the device is. 'OUI · VENDOR ONLY' means the block belongs to the manufacturer, so it can tell you the maker, such as Hikvision or Axon, but not which of their products this is. 'OUI · CHIPSET ONLY' means the block belongs to the maker of the radio chip inside the device. Flock uses that chip, but so do routers and home cameras. this label also means the name and service IDs did not match. in both cases the app shows a CONFIRM IT checklist: look around, and check whether the device is still there on a second pass.

whatever the number, a match means a radio that fits a known signature is turned on nearby. it does not mean a camera is recording, or that it is pointed at you.

questions.q: Why doesn't the beacon pick up ALPR cameras very often?
questions.a:
the detector listens for Flock cameras that broadcast over bluetooth or 2.4 GHz wifi, and for Raven audio sensors over bluetooth only. many current installs use neither, as the note next to the switch in Beacon settings says. a drive with no ALPR detections is normal and does not mean your beacon has a fault.

the beacon does detect a device when it recognizes one of these: a matching broadcast name, an address in Flock's own hardware address block, or an external battery pack's broadcast name. those detections are real, but they happen only occasionally. confirm a detection by eye, and do not use detections to count the cameras you drove past.

the Map also has a community-mapped ALPR layer (known ALPR cameras in Map options), which is on by default. its rings are mapped locations, not live detections, and they are the more reliable way to see where cameras have been logged. a ring and a nearby detection do not confirm each other.

questions.q: The ALPR map shows a camera here, but the beacon isn't detecting it. Is it broken?
questions.a:
no. the hollow rings come from a separate community-mapped ALPR reference dataset. detection pins come from signals your beacon heard, and they can be recent or historical depending on the active, recent, or all choice at the top of the Map. neither layer confirms the other.

a camera may send its data over a cellular connection, be out of range, or not broadcast anything the beacon recognizes. the community record may also be incomplete or out of date. a detection near a ring, even an emphasized ring, only shows that the beacon heard a matching signal nearby. it does not prove the signal came from that exact mapped camera. a pin without a ring does not automatically mean you found a new camera either.

Map options has settings for the reference layer and for extra mapped entries. attribution or tier labels describe the source record. they do not show how confident a live detection is. if you know a device was broadcasting and the beacon missed it, use improve detection to prepare a capture you can choose to share.

questions.q: What does a body camera detection mean?
questions.a:
it only means that a radio matching a known body cam signature is turned on nearby. it does not mean a camera is recording. the broadcast does not include recording status, so the beacon cannot tell a camera that is recording from one sitting in its mount. the detector was validated against body cams worn by officers on normal patrol.

four different signatures are all reported as a body cam detection, and they are not equally strong, so each detection shows which one matched. 'BWC DEVICE' is a tag that Axon body cams include in their broadcast. the tag is in the advertisement data and does not depend on the address, so it still matches when the device randomizes its address. it is the strongest signature the beacon has. 'Axon OUI' means the address is in Axon's own block but the tag is missing, so the device is Axon equipment of some kind. Axon also uses this block for docks and other products. 'Utility BodyWorn' matches either the device's broadcast name, where the camera identifies itself, or the address block alone, which is a weaker match. 'Motorola Solutions OUI' is a vendor-level match, not a camera signature. the block belongs to Motorola Solutions, which also uses it for two-way radios, docks, and site equipment.

check the signature line, because the category word alone does not tell you which signature matched. the Motorola match has its own switch under body cams in Beacon settings. it is off by default because in one capture at an airport, none of its 27 matches were body cameras.

questions.q: A drone kept showing up after it landed or was turned off. Is that real?
questions.a:
it can be. Remote ID comes from the drone, not the controller or your phone. in the US the FAA requires drones to broadcast Remote ID from takeoff until shutdown, so a powered-on drone left on the ground can keep broadcasting. rules differ outside the US. the aircraft has its own battery and power button, so closing the drone's app or turning off the controller does not turn it off. on DJI drones, one short press may not turn the drone off. to turn it off, press the power button once, then press and hold.

open the detection and expand Technical details. if there is a Status row, it shows 'On ground', 'Airborne', 'Emergency', or 'System fault'. 'System fault' means the drone's Remote ID system has failed. the drone reports this status itself, and the beacon only updates it when the drone sends a position. 'On ground' on a detection that is still updating means the drone is powered on and transmitting. 'Airborne' means the drone reports it is flying. a drone can fly on its own after losing contact with its controller. if there is no Status row, you cannot tell whether the drone is flying or on the ground.

none of this tells you whether the camera is recording. Remote ID does not include recording status, and a powered drone on the ground can still record.

to see whether the drone is still broadcasting, watch the Status screen. it removes a device about 45 seconds after the beacon stops receiving its signal. the Map's recent view keeps a pin at the last known position for about 15 minutes, so a pin on the map does not mean the drone is still broadcasting.

a Detail ending in 'gear, no Remote ID' is a different kind of detection. it matched only a drone maker's address block, which the maker's controllers and other gear can also use. these detections have no Status row or aircraft position. detection by address block alone is off by default, and desert mode turns it on.

questions.q: Can it find a hidden camera in an airbnb or hotel room?
questions.a:
sometimes. turn on the network cameras detector and the beacon flags nearby wifi devices whose hardware addresses belong to supported camera vendors. a match shows the vendor, not the device, so it could be a doorbell, a recorder, a disclosed camera, or another product from the same maker.

it cannot detect wired, analog, cellular-only, powered-off, or 5 GHz-only cameras, cameras that stay idle until they sense motion, or unknown cameras that do not send out a recognizable signal. it does not detect lenses or infrared light. an empty scan does not mean the room is clean. use the beacon together with a physical sweep: check smoke detectors, vents, and mirrors, use a flashlight to look for reflections from a camera lens, and look through your phone camera in the dark for infrared lights.

questions.q: How far away can it hear something?
questions.a:
range is usually tens of meters, not whole neighborhoods. with a clear line of sight outdoors, a pole-mounted device may reach close to 100 meters. walls, vehicles, clothing, and bags can reduce that to a few meters. wifi often carries farther than bluetooth, and a device with a proper antenna on a pole reaches farther than a body cam under a jacket.

placement matters too: the beacon detects more on a dashboard than inside a backpack. use it to see what is around you right now. if nothing shows up, no device the beacon recognizes was broadcasting within range. other devices can still be nearby.

questions.q: What does the signal number mean, and why is a weak signal not the same as far away?
questions.a:
the number in a detection's SIGNAL panel is RSSI, in dBm. it shows how strong the device's signal was when the beacon received it. it is always negative, and closer to zero is stronger, so -45 is much stronger than -90. the graph below it plots the same number over time. it goes up as you get closer and down as you move away. the graph uses the same fixed scale for every device, with STRONG at the top and WEAK at the bottom.

RSSI does not measure distance. each radio sets its own transmit power, and that affects the number much more than distance does. a pole-mounted camera or a drone on wifi transmits at high power and can show a strong signal from across a street. smart glasses and tracking tags transmit at low power on bluetooth to save battery, so they can be a few meters away and still show a weak signal. a jacket over a body cam weakens its signal further.

compare a device to its own earlier readings, not to other devices. as you move, watch whether that device's line goes up. between two devices, a stronger number does not mean that one is closer. the Log's strongest sort and the map pin both use raw RSSI, so neither tells you which device is nearest.

questions.q: How long does the battery last?
questions.a: roughly 4 to 7 hours of continuous scanning on a charge, depending on how many devices are nearby: about 4 hours in busy areas with lots of devices and up to 7 hours somewhere quiet. eco mode extends that by running the wifi scans less often, while bluetooth scanning stays on full-time. the slim model has no battery and runs as long as it's connected to a suitable USB power source. on a power bank, runtime depends on the bank's capacity.

questions.q: Why does the battery percentage jump around?
questions.a:
the battery model doesn't have a dedicated fuel-gauge chip, so it estimates charge from voltage. the radios draw power in bursts, so heavy scanning can lower the voltage and make the percentage drop a few points. it goes back up when the load eases off. lithium battery voltage also stays fairly flat through the middle of a charge, so the estimate changes faster near full and near empty.

the firmware smooths the reading, but a few percent of drift is normal. the percentage tells you whether the battery is full, half, or getting low, but it is not exact.

questions.q: Where does my data go?
questions.a:
detections are stored on your phone. the offline buffer is optional and stores records on the beacon while your phone is not connected. neither one is uploaded automatically. the only network requests the app makes on its own are for map tiles, firmware update checks and downloads, and the community ALPR dataset. the ALPR layer is on by default, and you can turn it off with the known ALPR cameras switch in Map options.

update and dataset downloads do not include your location, map view, or detections, but the server still sees the request and your IP address, as with any download. map tile requests let the tile provider see the area you are viewing. they do not include detections. exports and improve detection reports are sent only when you choose to share them. opening the help built into the app does not make any network requests. external help links open in your browser.

questions.q: Does the app need access to my files or storage?
questions.a:
the app does not need a broad storage permission. Log exports and improve detection reports are files the app writes in its own private storage. when you share one, the system share sheet or a mail compose screen opens and you choose where it goes. nothing is uploaded automatically.

the app's own copy of each export is temporary. when a copy is more than an hour old, the app deletes it the next time it starts (on android, also the next time you export). clearing the Log deletes all of those copies immediately, so if you need an export as evidence, save it or send it somewhere outside the app first. a copy you saved or sent elsewhere is not affected.

clearing the Log also removes the app's detection notifications. on android it also deletes the cached map tiles, because they show which areas you viewed. those tiles are kept only in the app's private internal storage, up to about 100 MB. on iphone the map is Apple Maps, which manages its own cache, so the app has no tile cache to clear. clearing the Log does not erase the board's offline buffer, which has its own Erase control under Beacon.

if you attach a photo to an improve detection report, you choose it with the system photo picker. this does not give the app access to your whole photo library. the app re-encodes the selected image to remove embedded metadata before it attaches it. anything visible in the image can still identify a person or place, so check what the photo shows as well.

questions.q: Why does the app want my location?
questions.a:
location is used for observation pins, tracker breadcrumbs, and place mutes within 50 meters. on iPhone, Live Mode also needs it to run in the background. Android 8 through 11 needs the Location permission to scan for bluetooth. newer Android versions use the Nearby devices permission for the connection instead. Android Live Mode does not request background Location.

your phone sends its current fix to your beacon over encrypted bluetooth. if your phone disconnects, buffered detections other than drones may use that last fix until it is about 18 hours old. restarting the beacon clears the fix. these locations show where your phone last was, not where the beacon went later.

regular Log exports can include observation, aircraft, and operator coordinates, and there is no setting to leave location out. improve detection has separate switches: your observation location and operator location are off by default, and aircraft location is on by default. opening a map also requests tiles from Apple Maps on iPhone or OpenStreetMap on Android. the map provider sees the area you are viewing and your IP address. your detections are not sent. on iPhone and newer Android versions you can decline Location and still get detections and keep a Log, but location features will be limited.

questions.q: Does a pin show where the camera is, or where I was?
questions.a:
for most detections, the pin uses the strongest signal sample that also had a usable observation location. a later sample with a location and a stronger RSSI moves the pin, and an equal or weaker one does not. a strong signal without a location does not move the pin. the pin estimates where the beacon heard the device best, not where the device is. the device was somewhere within range of that point.

tracker details can also show a breadcrumb trail of your observation positions for the session. offline records may instead use the last fix your phone sent before it disconnected. that fix does not update if the beacon is moved without your phone.

the exception is a Remote ID drone that broadcasts valid aircraft or operator coordinates. those positions come from the broadcast. a drone matched only by vendor does not give an aircraft GPS position, even though it is in the drone category.

questions.q: Do I need an account or a subscription?
questions.a: no. there's no account, cloud, fee, or telemetry. you buy the beacon once, and the app is free forever.

questions.q: What happens if soyboi disappears tomorrow?
questions.a: local scanning and your saved Log work without an account or a connection to our servers. the source code for the app and the ESP32-S3 firmware is on GitHub, so others can maintain it. new firmware downloads and community-map dataset updates come from online servers, so they could stop if those servers go offline. map tiles also depend on third-party providers. the beacon keeps detecting devices with the signatures it already has.

questions.q: Does it get better over time?
questions.a:
detection improves through firmware and app updates. there is no automatic learning on the board. the app checks for compatible firmware and offers the update over bluetooth, and you choose whether to install it. on supported beacons, one update can cover both radios. you can also update over USB with the web flasher. new app features and in-app FAQ changes come with app updates.

if the beacon missed a device, open improve detection under Beacon to capture what the beacon sees nearby, choose the location options, add a photo if you want, then tap Review & Share. you confirm where the report goes and send it from your mail or sharing app. no report is sent automatically.

questions.q: Is the hardware open source too?
questions.a: the app and the ESP32-S3 firmware are fully open source, and always will be. the nRF scanner firmware and the board design are not published. you buy the hardware, and you own all the data it produces.
